records.name: Van
records.summary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for this province. That absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence, not local permissiveness: the nationwide framework applies in full.

As documented nationally: an October 2025 draft judicial package would criminalise conduct judged contrary to biological sex or general morality (up to three years) and same-sex ceremonies (up to four), bar gender-affirming care below age 25 behind an infertility assessment, and expose patients and providers to prosecution — protested by civic groups and the medical association. The national LGBTI monitor's 2025 report describes hostility as explicit state policy: 'family' directives to public institutions, a first organisational closure in years, 3 hate-motivated killings, 89 ill-treatment violations, 299 detention decisions. July 2025 brought mass identity-check roundups in which police detained trans women and recorded names and images without stated grounds.

records.name: Yozgat
records.summary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for this province. That absence records the absence of documented divergence — not local safety — because the national rules apply here unchanged.

Those rules, as documented: a judicial package leaked in October 2025 would criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality (up to three years) and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to four); raise the minimum age for gender-affirming healthcare from 18 to 25 behind a permanent-infertility mandate with state-hospital evaluations; and expose patients (up to three years) and providers (up to seven) to charges — protested by 15 LGBTI groups and the national medical association, with regional-court precedent cited against it. The country's longest-running LGBTI monitor's 2025 report describes hostility becoming explicit state policy: presidential-centred 'family' directives to public institutions, the first closure of an LGBTI organisation in years, 6 right-to-life violations (3 hate-motivated killings), 89 torture or ill-treatment violations (51 in 2024), 313 liberty violations with 299 detention decisions, private-life violations rising 16 to 67 including blocked hormone therapy, 61 travel bans, expression violations 216 to 540, and 336 assembly violations.

records.name: Şırnak
records.summary: No Şırnak-specific trans statute, enforcement series or incident pattern was found in this pass. The prior estimate flags this province as a far-south-east conflict zone, but the three sources here contain no provincial evidence either way — so the record rests entirely on the country-wide picture: a leaked October 2025 judicial package would criminalise conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' (up to 3 years) and same-sex ceremonies (up to 4 years), raise the minimum age for gender-affirming healthcare to 25 with a permanent-infertility mandate, and expose patients (up to 3 years) and providers (up to 7 years) to charges; the 2025 national monitoring report recorded 6 right-to-life violations (3 hate-motivated killings), 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (51 in 2024), 313 liberty violations with 299 detention decisions, and 'Year of the Family' directives driving rainbow-symbol bans with expression violations rising from 216 to 540. Where a province is marked by armed conflict and heavy security presence, no-documentation should be read as least-likely-to-document rather than least-likely-to-occur.

As with every no-signal province here, the absence of documentation means absence of local divergence, not local safety.

records.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
records.summary: Direction: mixed — the most legally protective jurisdiction in Latin America, with a repeating pattern of police round-ups of travestis and trans women in one neighbourhood. The city has operated its own anti-discrimination law since 1996, hosts a large visible scene and an LGBTQ-driven tourism economy, and concentrates the administration of the national employment-quota law for travesti, trans and transgender people alongside the national femicide/travesticide registry — it is where state response is most likely to be present. Against that: on 18 September, six months after an unlawful detention, officers from police station 18 carried out fresh detentions, arrests and arbitrary identifications of travestis and trans women in the Constitución neighbourhood, writing several up under article 81 of the City's Contravention Code for lacking documents and arresting one — activists describe it as 'a new illegal procedure against travestis and trans', the third-plus iteration of the same operation in the same barrio, making it a pattern rather than a single incident.
